Welcome to Battles of History. Today we are learning about the battle for Pegasus Bridge, which happened on the night of the fifth to the Sixth of June 1944, between the British Sixth Airborne Division and the German army defending Normandy.

PEGASUS BRIDGE. Night of 5 to 6 June nineteen forty-four , Bay-noo-veel, Normandy. The first fight of D-Day, and one of the most precise operations of the war: six gliders, 181 men, two bridges, and sixteen minutes past midnight. The British side wrote it up in detail and the men told it for fifty years. The German side is thinner: a coastal division's records and a few veterans. The tags show which is which.

Why two bridges mattered. The Allied landings of 6 June nineteen forty-four put five armies on the beaches of Normandy. The eastern end of the line was Sword Beach, and east of Sword ran two waterways side by side from Kahn to the sea: the Kahn Canal and the River Orn. The only crossings between Kahn and the coast were two bridges on the road from Bay-noo-veel to Rahn-veel, a few hundred metres apart. If the British held them, the German armour east of the Orn could not reach the beaches, and the airborne division dropped east of the river could be reinforced. If the Germans blew them, that division was cut off. The bridges had to be taken intact, by surprise, before the Germans could fire the demolition charges. That meant gliders, landing in silence, within yards of the targets, in the dark.

The British force. The task went to D Company of the second Ox and Bucks, an airlanding battalion of the 6th Airborne Division, under Major John Howard: 139 of his own men, thirty sappers of the Royal Engineers, and twelve glider pilots of the Glider Pilot Regiment. 181 men in six Hor-sas, three for each bridge. The glider pilots were the key. Staff Sergeant Jim Wall-work, flying the lead glider, had to put thirty men down in a field the size of a football pitch, in the dark, beside a bridge, by stopwatch and compass alone. He did it to within fifty yards. Air Chief Marshal Leigh-Mallory called it the finest feat of flying of the war. Behind them came the seventh Parachute Battalion, dropping north of Rahn-veel at fifty minutes past midnight to take over the bridges, and, from the beach at dawn, Lord Luvvat's first Special Service Brigade of commandos, due to march the six miles from Sword and relieve them by noon. The men carried Sten guns, Bren guns, grenades and the pee-at, a spring-loaded anti-tank projector with a range of a hundred yards. Howard had one pee-at team per platoon and no artillery at all.

The German garrison. The bridges were guarded by about fifty men of the 716th Infantry Division, a coastal-defence formation of older men and conscripts from across occupied Europe, under Major Hans Shmitt, with a 50 millimetre anti-tank gun, machine guns in trenches, and the bridges wired for demolition. The explosives were not in place. The charges were stored nearby and were to be fitted when an attack was expected. Nobody expected one that night: the weather was bad, the sentries were two, and the garrison was asleep in the village. Ten miles away lay the 21st Panzer Division, the only armoured division near the coast, with more than a hundred Panzer four tanks. Its orders were to counter-attack any landing, but it could not move without permission from above, and permission did not come for hours. How many Germans fought at the bridges in the night is not recorded. Our garrison and the tanks that came are a reconstruction from the two accounts.

The ground. The canal bridge was a steel lifting bridge, a bass-cule, with a counterweight tower at its west end, carrying the road from Bay-noo-veel on the west bank to the strip of land between the waterways. The river bridge, four hundred yards east, was a plain girder bridge to Rahn-veel. Between the canal and the river lay flat marshy pasture cut by ditches and a pond: landing zone X, where three gliders were to land nose to the canal bridge. East of the river bridge lay landing zone Y. The villages of Bay-noo-veel and Luh Por stood on the west bank, Rahn-veel on the east. Our map is a reconstruction from the sketch maps in Howard's report and the regimental history: one pixel to a metre, with the villages, the tower and the gun pit where the accounts put them.

Dead-stick. The operation was named Dead-stick, the pilots' word for landing with no engine. The gliders cast off over the coast at seven minutes past midnight and came down through cloud, turning twice by stopwatch, to arrive out of the dark at ninety miles an hour, braked by a parachute and a skid. The first glider hit the ground at sixteen minutes past midnight, forty-seven yards from the canal bridge. The second and third followed within a minute. At the river bridge two of three arrived; the sixth, released in the wrong place, landed eight miles away on the wrong river. Sixteen minutes past midnight. Out of the dark at ninety miles an hour, the first Hor-sa hits the ground, bounces, smashes through the wire and stops with its nose forty-seven yards from the canal bridge. The second and third land within a minute. Nobody on the bridge has heard a thing.

The gliders were released at 6000 feet over the coast and flew seven miles by stopwatch, making two timed turns in cloud. Wall-work, in the lead, aimed for the wire at the end of the field to stop the glider before the embankment: he hit it, and the two pilots went through the windscreen. Everyone aboard was stunned for a few seconds; some of the men thought they were dead.

Brother-ridge's platoon is out of the wreck and running for the bridge. A sentry fires a flare; the platoon charges across, firing from the hip, grenades into the pillbox and the trenches. Brother-ridge is hit by a burst from the machine gun at the far end and falls at the west bank. The bridge is taken in three minutes.

The plan was speed: no stealth after the landing, just the shortest run to the bridge before the sentries could reach the detonator. Corporal Bailey put a grenade through the slit of the pillbox; Lieutenant Wood's platoon cleared the trenches on the east bank. Den Brother-ridge, hit in the neck, died within the hour, the first Allied soldier killed by enemy fire on D-Day.

Four hundred yards east, two gliders have landed beside the river bridge. Fox's platoon rushes it; a machine gun fires a few bursts and the crew run. Sweeney's platoon arrives at the run from a field seven hundred yards short. The sappers report the demolition chambers empty. Howard's radio sends the code words: Ham, the canal bridge; Jam, the river bridge. Both taken intact.

The explosives were stored in a shed and had never been fitted to the bridges, against standing orders, because the garrison did not expect an attack. The sappers cut every wire they could find anyway. The sixth glider, Priday's, had been cast off in the wrong place and landed on the River Deev, eight miles away; its platoon fought its way back over two days.

A staff car and a motorcycle come down the road from Rahn-veel at speed: Major Shmitt, commanding the bridge garrison, returning from an evening in the town. The British at the river bridge shoot up both. Shmitt is wounded and captured, and tells his captors in good English that they will all be thrown back into the sea.

Shmitt was the one German officer who knew the demolition plan. Captured within fifteen minutes of the landing, he could not raise the alarm or order the charges fitted. The German side had no commander at the bridges for the rest of the night; the counter-attacks that came were organised from outside.

Half an hour later the sky to the north-east fills with the seventh Parachute Battalion, dropping to take over the bridges. The drop is scattered by wind and flak; companies land miles apart and in the flooded fields. A third of the battalion will never reach the rendezvous.

The 6th Airborne Division dropped east of the Orn to seal off the flank of the invasion. The seventh Battalion's job was the bridges, and it got there, but with 200 men instead of 600, and without its mortars and machine guns, which had come down in the water. Howard's company would have to hold longer than planned.

Engines in Bay-noo-veel. Two tanks of the 21st Panzer Division come up the road from the south with infantry behind them, toward the T-junction a hundred yards from the bridge. Sergeant Thornton is in a ditch at the junction with the company's last pee-at and two bombs. He lets the lead tank come to thirty yards and fires. It stops, burns, and its ammunition explodes for the next hour.

The pee-at was a spring-loaded tube that threw a three-pound bomb a hundred yards, and it was feared for its unreliability. Thornton later said he was shaking so much he was sure he would miss. The burning tank lit the crossroads and blocked the road; the second tank withdrew, and the Germans, hearing the explosions, believed the British had anti-tank guns. No tank tried the road again that night.

Howard's platoons hold the crossroads, the café and the trenches on both banks. German patrols probe from Bay-noo-veel and Luh Por and are driven off. The wounded are carried into the café, where the Gon-dray family hand out the champagne they have kept buried since nineteen forty.

Howard had fewer than 150 men to hold two bridges and the approaches on both sides, with no artillery. He pulled the platoons into tight positions at the bridge ends, kept the pee-at at the crossroads, and waited for the paratroopers. The German response was piecemeal: no one above the garrison knew yet what had happened.

Lieutenant Colonel Pine Coffin crosses the river bridge with what he has gathered of the seventh Battalion, about two hundred men, and takes over the position. A Company goes into Bay-noo-veel, B Company into Luh Por. Howard's company falls back to the bridges as the reserve.

From this point the bridges were held by a battalion rather than a company, but a weak one: no mortars, no machine guns, few radios. The paratroopers' task was to hold the west bank, the villages, so that the Germans could not reach the bridges with their guns. It was in the villages, not at the bridges, that most of the day's fighting happened.

First light. German infantry of the 21st Panzer Division attack Bay-noo-veel from the south with mortar fire, and press into the village. A Company of the paratroopers fights them house to house and holds. Snipers in the church tower at Luh Por pick at anyone who moves on the bridge.

The 21st Panzer Division had finally been released, but its main body was sent west of the Orn toward the beaches, not at the bridges. What came to Bay-noo-veel was a battalion-sized attack supported by mortars, enough to press the paratroopers hard for several hours but not to break through to the bridge.

Two German gunboats come down the canal from Weest-ray-am, the leading one firing a 20 millimetre cannon at the bridge. A pee-at bomb from the east bank hits it below the wheelhouse; it slews into the bank and its crew are taken prisoner. The second boat turns back for the sea.

The boats were from the naval base at Weest-ray-am, sent to find out what was happening at the bridge. It was the second time that morning the pee-at, the weapon nobody trusted, had decided a fight. The commandos landing on Sword at that moment were four hours away.

A German fighter-bomber comes in low along the canal and drops a bomb on the canal bridge. It hits the tower, bounces off, and falls into the water without exploding. The bridge is not touched again from the air.

A hit would have cut the road to the beaches for the airborne division. The dud was pure luck, and both accounts record it. Through the morning the Germans tried the bridge with tanks, infantry, a gunboat, snipers and an aircraft, and every attempt was too small and too late.

The attacks on Bay-noo-veel slacken. The paratroopers are down to half strength in the village and have lost most of their officers, but the Germans have not reached the bridge. From the north comes the sound of the fighting at Sword, and then, faintly, bagpipes.

Luvvat's brigade had landed at eight forty and fought its way through Coll-veel and the gun batteries behind the beach. Luvvat had promised Howard he would be at the bridge by noon. He was two minutes late, and apologised for it.

At one o'clock Lord Luvvat's commandos come down the road from Luh Por, green berets instead of helmets, Piper Bill Millin playing Blue Bonnets over the Border at their head. They cross the canal bridge under sniper fire at a walk, as Luvvat ordered, losing several men on the span, and shake hands with the airborne on the far side.

Luvvat marched his men across at the walk, pipes playing, as a point: the beach and the bridge were joined. The snipers in Luh Por were still active and the crossing cost lives. Howard's report records the relief at one o'clock; Luvvat's own account says one oh two and apologises for the delay.

The commandos cross the river bridge to Rahn-veel and the rest of the brigade follows through the afternoon. In the evening the Warwickshires of the third Division arrive from the beach to take over the bridges, and Howard's company marches to Rahn-veel. It has lost two killed and fourteen wounded on the bridges. The seventh Battalion has lost sixty.

The bridges stayed in British hands for the rest of the campaign and the 6th Airborne Division held the flank east of the Orn for two months. The canal bridge was renamed Pegasus after the airborne badge; the river bridge, later, Hor-sa. Howard's company fought on in Normandy until September, and lost many more.

Both bridges were taken intact within a quarter of an hour of the landing and held until the commandos arrived at one o'clock and the third Division in the evening. D Company lost two killed, Brother-ridge and Lance-Corporal Greenhalgh, who drowned in the pond, and fourteen wounded in the assault. The seventh Parachute Battalion lost about sixty killed and wounded holding Bay-noo-veel and Luh Por. German losses at the bridges are not recorded; the garrison was scattered, one tank and one gunboat destroyed, and the counter-attacks turned back. The 21st Panzer Division, the only armour near the coast, was held back for hours by the chain of command and then sent west of the Orn. The bridges kept its eastern half from the beaches. The canal bridge was renamed Pegasus Bridge in nineteen forty-four after the badge of the airborne forces. Howard, Wall-work and Luvvat came back every June for the rest of their lives; the café is still run by the Gon-dray family.

Welcome to Battles of History. Today we are learning about the Battle of Waterloo, which happened on the eighteenth of June 1815, between Wellington's Allied army with Bloocher's Prussians, and Napoleon's French army.

BATTLE OF WATERLOO. Napoleon had escaped from Elba and returned to power. He had 100 days, and this was the battle that decided them. The Allied army and the Prussians had been driven apart two days before. Wellington took the ridge at Mon San Zhon; Bloocher was coming to join him. This introduction separates what the sources say from what historians have reconstructed. Watch for the coloured tags.

The ridge. Wellington placed most of his infantry on the reverse slope of the ridge, out of sight and out of the range of the French guns. The sunken road along the crest, bordered by hedges, was the line the French had to reach. Oogoomon, a walled farm complex, stood on the Allied right. La Hay Sant, a farm on the Brussels road, stood in the centre. It had rained hard all night. The French attack did not begin until the late morning, when the ground had dried a little.

The French army. Napoleon massed the guns of the army in a grand battery opposite the centre-left of the Allied line. The number of guns is disputed: sources give between about forty and eighty. D'Erlon's infantry corps attacked the Allied left. Later in the afternoon, kweerasseers and lancers charged the Allied right-centre again and again. The French army numbered about 72,000, the Allied about 68,000, and the Prussians about 50,000. These are common estimates; the sources do not agree.

The Prussians. Bloocher had been beaten at Leenyee two days before. His army withdrew, and then came toward Waterloo. The first Prussians, Boolow's corps, reached the French right in the late afternoon. The exact time is disputed; the sources give between about 16 30 and 17 hundred. Napoleon had sent Marshal Grooshee with about 33,000 men to follow the Prussians. Grooshee fought their rearguard at Wahvruh and never reached Waterloo.

The sources. Many of the stories of this battle were written by the men who lived through it, decades afterwards. Some were written to defend a commander's reputation. The French side has its own collection of eyewitness accounts, many published for the first time in recent years. Where a story is famous but not confirmed, the Record says so.

Wellington's infantry lies on the reverse slope. The guns stand on the crest. The French army waits on the far side of the valley.
Why the reverse slope? Infantry behind the crest could not be shelled. They could stand up and fire when the French came over the top.
The battle opens at Oogoomon, on the Allied right, in the late morning. Ray's infantry attacks the walled farm, and the fighting there goes on all day.

Many historians think the attack was meant to draw in Wellington's reserves. Instead it drew in more and more French battalions. The defenders closed the north gate after the French forced it: a famous story, told differently by different witnesses.
The French grand battery fires on the Allied line. The number of guns is disputed.
Napoleon massed the guns to break the Allied line before the infantry attack. How many guns there were, and how much damage they did, is not agreed.
D'Erlon's corps advances against the Allied left-centre, east of the Brussels road. Picton's division meets it at the hedges along the crest.
D'Erlon's divisions advanced in unusually broad, deep formations, which were slow to deploy and made big targets. Sir Thomas Picton was killed leading the counter-attack.
Uxbridge sends the heavy cavalry over the crest. The Union Brigade, with the Scots Greys, breaks dairlon's attack and captures two eagles.
Carried away, the cavalry rode on into the grand battery and was cut up by French lancers and kweerasseers. How far it got, and how many guns it put out of action, is disputed.
Marshal Nay sends wave after wave of kweerasseers and lancers up the slope between Oogoomon and La Hay Sant, against the Allied right-centre.
Why Nay attacked is disputed: he may have taken movement behind the crest for a retreat. The charges went in without infantry to support them.
The Allied infantry forms square. The French cavalry cannot break the squares, and falls back.
A square with bayonets outward was the infantry's answer to cavalry. Without infantry or guns to follow up, the cavalry could not break it.
Boolow's Prussians come in from the east and attack Plahnsenwah, on the French right. Lobo's corps is sent to hold them.
The Prussian arrival forced Napoleon to commit troops to his right, away from the centre. The exact time is disputed; the sources give between about 16 30 and 17 hundred.
Out of ammunition, the King's German Legion is driven out of La Hay Sant. French guns and skirmishers come up close to the centre of the Allied line.
Major Baring's men held the farm for most of the day, until their rifle ammunition ran out. With the farm lost, the Allied centre was at its weakest of the day.
Tseeten's Prussian corps reaches Wellington's far left. The Allied light cavalry on that flank can now move to the centre.
Tseeten's arrival freed Vivian's and Vandeler's cavalry brigades to steady the Allied centre, shortly before the Imperial Guard attacked.
The Imperial Guard goes forward in the last French attack. Wellington's reserves meet it on the crest.
The Guard's attack is the last throw of the day. The words attributed to its officers are disputed, and the Record does not repeat them as fact.
The French attack is broken. The Prussians press on, and the French army retreats south. Napoleon abdicated three days later.
The battle ended the Napoleonic Wars. Its result is not in doubt; the detail of who did what, and when, is what the sources argue about.

The French attacks on the ridge failed, and the Prussians came in on the French right. Napoleon's army broke and retreated south. Napoleon abdicated three days later, and the Napoleonic Wars ended. The sources give very different casualty figures. Historians treat them as estimates. The stories of the day, such as the Oogoomon gate and the Scots Greys charge, are told from both sides, and not always accurately.

Welcome to Battles of History. Today we are learning about the Battle of Gowguhmeeluh, which happened in 331 B C E, between the Macedonian army of Aligzander the Great and the Persian army of Duhryus the Third.

BATTLE OF GAUGAMELA. 1 October 331 B C E , northern Mesopotamia. Aligzander III of Macedon and Duhryus III of Persia met on an open plain in northern Mesopotamia. It was the decisive battle of Aligzander's conquest of the Persian empire. This introduction separates what the ancient accounts say from what historians have reconstructed. Watch for the coloured tags.

Two kings, one empire. Aligzander had beaten Duhryus at Issus in 333 B C E, taken the Levant and Egypt, and crossed the Euphrates. Duhryus had gathered an army from across the empire to stop him. Duhryus chose the ground. He had the plain levelled, so that his cavalry and scythed chariots could work at full speed. The site itself is not known. The ancient accounts do not fix it, and modern scholars still disagree about where it lay.

The Macedonian army. The Macedonians were about 40,000 foot and 7,000 horse. These are common modern estimates; no ancient source gives a reliable count. The phalanx of pezetyroy, with their long suhrissuh pikes, formed the centre. Aligzander commanded the right, with the Companion cavalry and the highpuhspists beside him. Parmenyon held the left with the Thessalian horse. Light troops and javelinmen screened the army and filled the gaps between units. They were the answer to the scythed chariots.

The Persian army. Airreeun gives the Persian army a million infantry and 40,000 cavalry. Historians reject these figures as exaggerated. Duhryus almost certainly had far more cavalry than Aligzander. Airreeun reports 200 scythed chariots and about 15 elephants. The chariots are well attested; the elephants were not shown fighting in any account we can rely on. Persian cavalry from Bactria and Saka lands stood on Duhryus's left, opposite Aligzander. Armenian and Cappadocian horse were on his right, opposite Parmenyon.

The sources. Our main account is Airreeun, writing about four centuries after the battle. He drew on lost histories, including those of Tollumee and Airihstobyoolus, who were with Aligzander. Diodorus and Curtius tell the battle differently, and sometimes more dramatically. Where they disagree with Airreeun, this game says so. A Babylonian astronomical diary records the battle as a Mesopotamian scribe saw it. It is the nearest thing to a contemporary record. Its wording is disputed: it may say that the king's soldiers left him, or that the king left his soldiers.

Welcome to Battles of History. Today we are learning about the battle for Pegasus Bridge, which happened on the night of the fifth to the Sixth of June 1944, between the British Sixth Airborne Division and the German army defending Normandy.

PEGASUS BRIDGE. Night of 5 to 6 June nineteen forty-four , Bay-noo-veel, Normandy. The first fight of D-Day, and one of the most precise operations of the war: six gliders, 181 men, two bridges, and sixteen minutes past midnight. The British side wrote it up in detail and the men told it for fifty years. The German side is thinner: a coastal division's records and a few veterans. The tags show which is which.

Why two bridges mattered. The Allied landings of 6 June nineteen forty-four put five armies on the beaches of Normandy. The eastern end of the line was Sword Beach, and east of Sword ran two waterways side by side from Kahn to the sea: the Kahn Canal and the River Orn. The only crossings between Kahn and the coast were two bridges on the road from Bay-noo-veel to Rahn-veel, a few hundred metres apart. If the British held them, the German armour east of the Orn could not reach the beaches, and the airborne division dropped east of the river could be reinforced. If the Germans blew them, that division was cut off. The bridges had to be taken intact, by surprise, before the Germans could fire the demolition charges. That meant gliders, landing in silence, within yards of the targets, in the dark.

The British force. The task went to D Company of the second Ox and Bucks, an airlanding battalion of the 6th Airborne Division, under Major John Howard: 139 of his own men, thirty sappers of the Royal Engineers, and twelve glider pilots of the Glider Pilot Regiment. 181 men in six Hor-sas, three for each bridge. The glider pilots were the key. Staff Sergeant Jim Wall-work, flying the lead glider, had to put thirty men down in a field the size of a football pitch, in the dark, beside a bridge, by stopwatch and compass alone. He did it to within fifty yards. Air Chief Marshal Leigh-Mallory called it the finest feat of flying of the war. Behind them came the seventh Parachute Battalion, dropping north of Rahn-veel at fifty minutes past midnight to take over the bridges, and, from the beach at dawn, Lord Luvvat's first Special Service Brigade of commandos, due to march the six miles from Sword and relieve them by noon. The men carried Sten guns, Bren guns, grenades and the pee-at, a spring-loaded anti-tank projector with a range of a hundred yards. Howard had one pee-at team per platoon and no artillery at all.

The German garrison. The bridges were guarded by about fifty men of the 716th Infantry Division, a coastal-defence formation of older men and conscripts from across occupied Europe, under Major Hans Shmitt, with a 50 millimetre anti-tank gun, machine guns in trenches, and the bridges wired for demolition. The explosives were not in place. The charges were stored nearby and were to be fitted when an attack was expected. Nobody expected one that night: the weather was bad, the sentries were two, and the garrison was asleep in the village. Ten miles away lay the 21st Panzer Division, the only armoured division near the coast, with more than a hundred Panzer four tanks. Its orders were to counter-attack any landing, but it could not move without permission from above, and permission did not come for hours. How many Germans fought at the bridges in the night is not recorded. Our garrison and the tanks that came are a reconstruction from the two accounts.

The ground. The canal bridge was a steel lifting bridge, a bass-cule, with a counterweight tower at its west end, carrying the road from Bay-noo-veel on the west bank to the strip of land between the waterways. The river bridge, four hundred yards east, was a plain girder bridge to Rahn-veel. Between the canal and the river lay flat marshy pasture cut by ditches and a pond: landing zone X, where three gliders were to land nose to the canal bridge. East of the river bridge lay landing zone Y. The villages of Bay-noo-veel and Luh Por stood on the west bank, Rahn-veel on the east. Our map is a reconstruction from the sketch maps in Howard's report and the regimental history: one pixel to a metre, with the villages, the tower and the gun pit where the accounts put them.

Dead-stick. The operation was named Dead-stick, the pilots' word for landing with no engine. The gliders cast off over the coast at seven minutes past midnight and came down through cloud, turning twice by stopwatch, to arrive out of the dark at ninety miles an hour, braked by a parachute and a skid. The first glider hit the ground at sixteen minutes past midnight, forty-seven yards from the canal bridge. The second and third followed within a minute. At the river bridge two of three arrived; the sixth, released in the wrong place, landed eight miles away on the wrong river. Choose how to see it: watch the night unfold as the two sides tell it, or take command of the bridges, or of the garrison and the tanks that must take them back.

Sixteen minutes past midnight. Out of the dark at ninety miles an hour, the first Hor-sa hits the ground, bounces, smashes through the wire and stops with its nose forty-seven yards from the canal bridge. The second and third land within a minute. Nobody on the bridge has heard a thing.

The gliders were released at 6000 feet over the coast and flew seven miles by stopwatch, making two timed turns in cloud. Wall-work, in the lead, aimed for the wire at the end of the field to stop the glider before the embankment: he hit it, and the two pilots went through the windscreen. Everyone aboard was stunned for a few seconds; some of the men thought they were dead.

Brother-ridge's platoon is out of the wreck and running for the bridge. A sentry fires a flare; the platoon charges across, firing from the hip, grenades into the pillbox and the trenches. Brother-ridge is hit by a burst from the machine gun at the far end and falls at the west bank. The bridge is taken in three minutes.

The plan was speed: no stealth after the landing, just the shortest run to the bridge before the sentries could reach the detonator. Corporal Bailey put a grenade through the slit of the pillbox; Lieutenant Wood's platoon cleared the trenches on the east bank. Den Brother-ridge, hit in the neck, died within the hour, the first Allied soldier killed by enemy fire on D-Day.

Four hundred yards east, two gliders have landed beside the river bridge. Fox's platoon rushes it; a machine gun fires a few bursts and the crew run. Sweeney's platoon arrives at the run from a field seven hundred yards short. The sappers report the demolition chambers empty. Howard's radio sends the code words: Ham, the canal bridge; Jam, the river bridge. Both taken intact.

The explosives were stored in a shed and had never been fitted to the bridges, against standing orders, because the garrison did not expect an attack. The sappers cut every wire they could find anyway. The sixth glider, Priday's, had been cast off in the wrong place and landed on the River Deev, eight miles away; its platoon fought its way back over two days.

A staff car and a motorcycle come down the road from Rahn-veel at speed: Major Shmitt, commanding the bridge garrison, returning from an evening in the town. The British at the river bridge shoot up both. Shmitt is wounded and captured, and tells his captors in good English that they will all be thrown back into the sea.

Shmitt was the one German officer who knew the demolition plan. Captured within fifteen minutes of the landing, he could not raise the alarm or order the charges fitted. The German side had no commander at the bridges for the rest of the night; the counter-attacks that came were organised from outside.

Half an hour later the sky to the north-east fills with the seventh Parachute Battalion, dropping to take over the bridges. The drop is scattered by wind and flak; companies land miles apart and in the flooded fields. A third of the battalion will never reach the rendezvous.

The 6th Airborne Division dropped east of the Orn to seal off the flank of the invasion. The seventh Battalion's job was the bridges, and it got there, but with 200 men instead of 600, and without its mortars and machine guns, which had come down in the water. Howard's company would have to hold longer than planned.

Engines in Bay-noo-veel. Two tanks of the 21st Panzer Division come up the road from the south with infantry behind them, toward the T-junction a hundred yards from the bridge. Sergeant Thornton is in a ditch at the junction with the company's last pee-at and two bombs. He lets the lead tank come to thirty yards and fires. It stops, burns, and its ammunition explodes for the next hour.

The pee-at was a spring-loaded tube that threw a three-pound bomb a hundred yards, and it was feared for its unreliability. Thornton later said he was shaking so much he was sure he would miss. The burning tank lit the crossroads and blocked the road; the second tank withdrew, and the Germans, hearing the explosions, believed the British had anti-tank guns. No tank tried the road again that night.

Howard's platoons hold the crossroads, the café and the trenches on both banks. German patrols probe from Bay-noo-veel and Luh Por and are driven off. The wounded are carried into the café, where the Gon-dray family hand out the champagne they have kept buried since nineteen forty.

Howard had fewer than 150 men to hold two bridges and the approaches on both sides, with no artillery. He pulled the platoons into tight positions at the bridge ends, kept the pee-at at the crossroads, and waited for the paratroopers. The German response was piecemeal: no one above the garrison knew yet what had happened.

Lieutenant Colonel Pine Coffin crosses the river bridge with what he has gathered of the seventh Battalion, about two hundred men, and takes over the position. A Company goes into Bay-noo-veel, B Company into Luh Por. Howard's company falls back to the bridges as the reserve.

From this point the bridges were held by a battalion rather than a company, but a weak one: no mortars, no machine guns, few radios. The paratroopers' task was to hold the west bank, the villages, so that the Germans could not reach the bridges with their guns. It was in the villages, not at the bridges, that most of the day's fighting happened.

First light. German infantry of the 21st Panzer Division attack Bay-noo-veel from the south with mortar fire, and press into the village. A Company of the paratroopers fights them house to house and holds. Snipers in the church tower at Luh Por pick at anyone who moves on the bridge.

The 21st Panzer Division had finally been released, but its main body was sent west of the Orn toward the beaches, not at the bridges. What came to Bay-noo-veel was a battalion-sized attack supported by mortars, enough to press the paratroopers hard for several hours but not to break through to the bridge.

Two German gunboats come down the canal from Weest-ray-am, the leading one firing a 20 millimetre cannon at the bridge. A pee-at bomb from the east bank hits it below the wheelhouse; it slews into the bank and its crew are taken prisoner. The second boat turns back for the sea.

The boats were from the naval base at Weest-ray-am, sent to find out what was happening at the bridge. It was the second time that morning the pee-at, the weapon nobody trusted, had decided a fight. The commandos landing on Sword at that moment were four hours away.

A German fighter-bomber comes in low along the canal and drops a bomb on the canal bridge. It hits the tower, bounces off, and falls into the water without exploding. The bridge is not touched again from the air.

A hit would have cut the road to the beaches for the airborne division. The dud was pure luck, and both accounts record it. Through the morning the Germans tried the bridge with tanks, infantry, a gunboat, snipers and an aircraft, and every attempt was too small and too late.

The attacks on Bay-noo-veel slacken. The paratroopers are down to half strength in the village and have lost most of their officers, but the Germans have not reached the bridge. From the north comes the sound of the fighting at Sword, and then, faintly, bagpipes.

Luvvat's brigade had landed at eight forty and fought its way through Coll-veel and the gun batteries behind the beach. Luvvat had promised Howard he would be at the bridge by noon. He was two minutes late, and apologised for it.

At one o'clock Lord Luvvat's commandos come down the road from Luh Por, green berets instead of helmets, Piper Bill Millin playing Blue Bonnets over the Border at their head. They cross the canal bridge under sniper fire at a walk, as Luvvat ordered, losing several men on the span, and shake hands with the airborne on the far side.

Luvvat marched his men across at the walk, pipes playing, as a point: the beach and the bridge were joined. The snipers in Luh Por were still active and the crossing cost lives. Howard's report records the relief at one o'clock; Luvvat's own account says one oh two and apologises for the delay.

The commandos cross the river bridge to Rahn-veel and the rest of the brigade follows through the afternoon. In the evening the Warwickshires of the third Division arrive from the beach to take over the bridges, and Howard's company marches to Rahn-veel. It has lost two killed and fourteen wounded on the bridges. The seventh Battalion has lost sixty.

The bridges stayed in British hands for the rest of the campaign and the 6th Airborne Division held the flank east of the Orn for two months. The canal bridge was renamed Pegasus after the airborne badge; the river bridge, later, Hor-sa. Howard's company fought on in Normandy until September, and lost many more.

Both bridges were taken intact within a quarter of an hour of the landing and held until the commandos arrived at one o'clock and the third Division in the evening. D Company lost two killed, Brother-ridge and Lance-Corporal Greenhalgh, who drowned in the pond, and fourteen wounded in the assault. The seventh Parachute Battalion lost about sixty killed and wounded holding Bay-noo-veel and Luh Por. German losses at the bridges are not recorded; the garrison was scattered, one tank and one gunboat destroyed, and the counter-attacks turned back. The 21st Panzer Division, the only armour near the coast, was held back for hours by the chain of command and then sent west of the Orn. The bridges kept its eastern half from the beaches. The canal bridge was renamed Pegasus Bridge in nineteen forty-four after the badge of the airborne forces. Howard, Wall-work and Luvvat came back every June for the rest of their lives; the café is still run by the Gon-dray family.

You command D Company. Your gliders are coming in on the canal bridge; two more follow at the river bridge. Take both bridges before the garrison wakes, dig in on both banks, and hold until the paratroopers arrive in the night and the commandos at one in the afternoon. You have one pee-at and no artillery.

You command the German response. The bridge garrison is asleep, its commander is in Rahn-veel, and the charges are not fitted. The British are landing now. Retake a bridge and hold it, or drive the airborne off the west bank, before the commandos arrive from the beach at one in the afternoon. The 21st Panzer Division's tanks and infantry become yours as the night goes on.
